issues.item: Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible
issues.explanation: The profile is centered on witnessed trauma with triggers involving crowded places, conversation topics, and bus riding, plus appraisals of vigilance and outsider status. The anger-loss-of-control appraisal introduces a distinct perpetration/impulse-control theme that is not supported by the other selected triggers, memory, threat, or strategy items, making it clinically hard to place within the same formulation.

Avoiding sex is not well linked to the rest of the profile. There are no sexual trauma cues, intimacy-related triggers, body-related appraisals, or threat/memory items that would explain sex-specific avoidance. Relative to the rest of the selected items, this strategy appears disconnected and inconsistent with the formulation.

vignette: When Maria turned the corner onto Main Street that winter afternoon, the city’s usual hum of traffic felt like a roar. She was on her third bus of the day, carrying the same worn leather bag she had brought for work, when a sudden commotion erupted at the bus’s back. A man, eyes wild, shoved a fellow passenger to the floor and the two collided, shattering a glass bottle that splintered on the pavement. The impact of the crash of the glass, the sharp hiss of the bus’s brakes, and the sight of blood splashing on the passenger’s jacket were seared into Maria’s mind. For a 72‑year‑old network engineer who had spent decades monitoring data streams rather than people, the experience felt like a breach in the invisible firewall that had kept her life orderly. That day, as the bus pulled into the terminal, Maria felt her breath shallow and her heart pound. She left the city immediately, avoiding the bus terminal and the crowded downtown plaza, and she began to report that the thought of stepping onto a bus again would make her throat close. This sudden sensitivity to crowded places, the routine bus ride, and even the mention of traffic or violent incidents in conversation became her triggers. The very environments that once were ordinary became constant reminders that something dangerous could happen at any moment, which in turn sharpened her sense that the world was a perilous place. The more Maria was confronted with those triggers—her partner’s voice asking if she would take the bus to the grocery store, a coworker laughing about a car accident on the news—her constant vigilance grew. She started noticing the shadows on the ceiling tiles at the data‑center she worked in, the rhythm of the elevator doors, and even the way her own hands tightened around the mouse. “I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next,” she told herself, and this belief became the core of her negative appraisal. The feeling that she was permanently an outsider, that she could not rely on the safety of her routines, made every familiar street or conference room feel like a potential threat. The belief that the world was dangerous made the world a source of fear, turning ordinary social exchanges into high‑stakes encounters. To counter this, Maria began to employ a strategy she described as positive reframing, insisting on telling herself that “everything will be fine” whenever she sensed a spike in anxiety. She also deliberately avoided crowds, steering clear of the shopping center she had frequented in her twenties, the community events at the senior center, and even the hallway that connected her office to the break room. These avoidance tactics were her maladaptive strategies, and they were driven directly by her negative appraisals. The belief that she was unsafe pushed her to preemptively remove herself from places where the risk might materialize, thereby reinforcing her sense of danger. Every time she chose to stay home on a Saturday instead of attending her husband’s book club, the memory of a potential threat lingered, and the urge to avoid that very event site increased. The avoidance, in turn, kept her constantly on edge, ensuring that her vigilance never ebbed. As the months slipped by, Maria’s avoidance behaviors grew more entrenched. On a humid Thursday, she found herself on the office floor, her manager discussing a software deployment that involved a public data feed. The manager’s mention of “user traffic spikes” triggered a cascade of memories: the bus crash, the broken glass, the feeling of her chest constricting. Maria’s gaze flickered to the windows, to the hallway beyond the conference room, to the crowds that would later fill the hallway as colleagues returned from lunch. Her mind rushed to reassure her that it was safer to stay in her seat and that the world was still a dangerous place, which made the very idea of stepping into that hallway feel almost obscene. This tight loop of triggers, negative appraisals, and maladaptive avoidance had begun to infiltrate every corner of her life, from the network equipment she monitored at night to the conversation she had with her husband about the upcoming family reunion. It was the strain on her marriage, the growing distance between her and her husband, and the realization that she could no longer attend the quarterly team meetings she had always considered routine that finally brought Maria to her therapist’s office. She explained that the “world is dangerous” belief had made her feel perpetually unsafe, that she could no longer let her positive reframing override the fear that clung to every crowd or bus route. She was afraid of losing the relationships that mattered most, but she also hoped that understanding why she felt so trapped might help her reclaim a sense of safety and normalcy.
